title: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives
note: Acid derivatives react by nucleophilic acyl substitution: the nucleophile adds to C=O to give a tetrahedral intermediate, which then expels the leaving group. Reactivity runs acid chloride > anhydride > ester > amide, and reactions run downhill: a more reactive derivative can make a less reactive one, not the reverse.

read.title: Walking down the reactivity ladder
text: Carboxylic acids and their derivatives all carry a carbonyl carbon bonded to an electronegative group, Y. That group can leave, which gives this family its own reaction pattern. A nucleophile first adds to the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate. The C=O then reforms and pushes Y out. The net result is that the nucleophile takes the place of Y. Aldehydes and ketones begin the same way, but hydride and alkyl groups cannot leave, so they stop at the alcohol stage instead.

How fast the first step goes depends on how electron-poor the carbonyl carbon is. Chlorine withdraws electrons, so acid chlorides react fastest. The oxygen of an ester and, even more, the nitrogen of an amide donate a lone pair into the carbonyl, which calms it down. The order is acid chloride, then anhydride, then ester, then amide.

This ladder tells you which conversions work. An acid chloride readily becomes an anhydride, an ester, or an amide, but an amide cannot be turned straight back into an ester or acid chloride. To climb the ladder, chemists start from the acid itself and activate it, for example with thionyl chloride.
